I am old, but I have worked this land long enough to know I should not gamble too much. On 9 mu, I will still keep the farm diversified. I will put 6 mu into the usual winter wheat followed immediately by summer maize, and keep 3 mu in cotton. Wheat and maize give me food and steady income, and cotton gives me some cash if the price is decent. With only two people in the household, I need a plan that is manageable in labor and not too heavy on cash at one time. I have well irrigation, so I can protect wheat at the key stages, but pumping costs money, so I will irrigate according to crop stage, not casually.

For wheat, I will sow in early October on the 6 mu after a normal rotary tillage and base fertilizer application. I usually aim for a solid but not excessive stand. I will use an improved local variety, apply most phosphorus and potassium as base fertilizer, and split nitrogen between base and jointing. I have learned over many years that wheat here responds well to timely water at overwintering, jointing, and grain filling if the spring is dry. After wheat harvest in June, I will move quickly into summer maize on the same 6 mu. The turnaround is tight, so I will keep tillage light and use direct or minimal-till sowing if I can arrange it. For cotton on 3 mu, I will not chase very high yield because of labor and age. I will fertilize moderately, irrigate a couple of times if the stand is under stress, and control insects when pressure is visible. My main thinking this year is stability: enough fertilizer to avoid obvious yield loss, careful irrigation because well water costs money, and no big changes from what has worked on my fields.
